source_excerpt: October is the Cybersecurity Awareness Month, and it gives companies, government bodies, schools and everyday users a chance to check how well they are protecting themselves in an increasingly connected world. But this yearâs edition arrives at a very different point in the cybersecurity story. Industry leaders say 2026 comes at a completely different stage of cybersecurity development. While the basics have not changed, AI poses a greater risk and simply being aware of cyberthreats is no longer sufficient, because the threat landscape has changed drastically. Organisations now have to prepare for new kinds of attacks â that can operate at machine speed, that take advantage of flaws found by AI, that target interconnected digital ecosystems, and so on.Parag Khurana, Country Manager, India, Barracuda NetworksCybercriminals don't always need advanced techniques to succeed. More often, they're looking for the easiest route in, whether that's a weak password, an unpatched application, an exposed account or an employee caught off guard by a convincing phishing attempt. As organisations adopt AI and embrace new ways of working, the challenge is not just keeping pace with new threats, but reducing unnecessary opportunities for attackers. AI is helping cybercriminals make familiar attacks such as phishing, social engineering and identity-based attacks more convincing, scalable and difficult to spot. Security fundamentals, layered protection, employee awareness and responsible AI governance all play an important role in making attacks harder to execute and less likely to succeed. Together, these measures help build the cyber resilience organisations need to withstand and recover from evolving threats.Avaneesh Vats, vice president, Information Technology, Techno DigitalAs AI, cloud computing and automation become integral to Indiaâs digital economy, cybersecurity must extend beyond protecting data and networks to securing the critical infrastructure that keeps essential services running. Data centres and power systems are increasingly interconnected through IT, operational technology (OT) and intelligent monitoring platforms. However, their security priorities differ fundamentally. While traditional IT security emphasises confidentiality, integrity and availability (CIA), OT environments prioritise availability, integrity and confidentiality (AIC), as operational continuity and safety are paramount. As these environments converge, vulnerabilities in one system can potentially affect critical operations and service continuity.This Cybersecurity Awareness Month, the priority must shift from securing individual systems to building resilience across the entire infrastructure ecosystem. This calls for a secure-by-design approach, where cybersecurity is embedded into infrastructure architecture from the outset through network segmentation, continuous monitoring, secure access controls and tested incident response mechanisms. As AI becomes increasingly integrated into critical operations, human oversight remains essential, particularly where automated decisions influence power and cooling systems. Ultimately, cyber resilience is not just about preventing attacks but about designing infrastructure that can withstand disruptions and sustain critical operations.Mandy Andress, CISO, ElasticEach year, Cybersecurity Awareness Month brings the same reminders: use strong passwords, turn on MFA, and think before you click. They still matter, but this year I keep coming back to one thought: AI isnât just another item on the awareness list; itâs changing what security means. Models, API keys, and agent permissions are now high-value targets, and attackers noticed before most asset inventories did. Phishing emails no longer contain typos, and a voice call can sound exactly like your CFO. We need to train people to verify the process, not just spot mistakes.Agents are also a new kind of identity. When software can reason and act on its own, âwho has access to whatâ becomes much harder to answer. But defenders get leverage too, with AI compressing detection, investigation and response in ways I didnât expect to see this soon. What hasnât changed is that security is a team sport. AI governance canât sit only with security; it needs legal, IT and the business at the same table, with shared ownership. The organisations that come out ahead wonât be the ones that avoided disruption. Theyâll be the ones that learned from it and became stronger because of it.Dhananjay Ganjoo, Managing Director, India & SAARC, F5AI is changing the very nature of enterprise risk because it is no longer operating in isolation. Across Indian organisations, AI models and autonomous agents are becoming part of business-critical operations, connecting to applications, accessing sensitive data and increasingly making decisions in real time. While this creates opportunities for innovation, it also opens new avenues for attackers through malicious prompts, API abuse and unauthorised data access. Critical vulnerabilities can be exploited and weaponised by bad actors at the speed of AI, and the only way to fight this is to introduce AI-driven defense.We saw this threat escalate recently with PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619), a pair of catastrophic, unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerabilities that left defenders with zero lead time. With details leaked on October 20 before patches were ready, attackers immediately began exploiting the flaw in the wild.For sectors such as banking and healthcare, the response cannot be limited to detecting threats after they occur. Enterprises need greater visibility into how AI systems interact with sensitive information, stronger controls to identify unusual behaviour and the ability to stop malicious activity as it happens. These safeguards must work consistently across on-premises and cloud environments without disrupting critical services.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
